item.content:encoded:
Contributing to the Linux kernel is something that I wanted to do since I got interested in programming. I never did it (until now!) because it felt too big, it was not an easy decision to start contributing to one of the biggest and most important projects of the open source space. After having contributed to some other open source projects, I decided that it was time that I give Linux a try. After all, it is a piece of software that I use on daily basis, it aligns with my interests in systems programming and it is a project where I can learn a lot because it is built by experts.

So, the decision is made, but where do I begin? Searching on the internet how I could get started1 I found the Linux Kernel Mentorship Program and decided to apply.

Application Process

The application process requires you to complete “A Beginner’s Guide to Linux Kernel Development (LFD103)”, a free course by the Linux foundation that teaches you the basics of the kernel development process and how to interact with the community. Along with that, other tasks are given to you. I recommend you to take them seriously.

The program usually receives a lot of applications, and there are a lot of talented people out there, so I did not have high hopes of getting accepted. On 5th of June I received an e-mail confirming that I was accepted! I was thrilled!

The First Weeks

Even though I am used to get familiar with big new codebases, the Linux kernel is a different beast. The kernel is divided into several subsystems that manage a different aspects. At the beginning of the program, we are told to focus in two subsystems at most, and believe me, this is a very valuable piece of advice. The kernel is huge, and each subsystem has its own peculiarities and conventions. Focusing on various subsystems at the same time means learning a lot of different and new information at the same time.

At the beginning it is normal to feel a little bit lost. A common question arises among mentees “What subsystems do I choose?”. My recommendation here is, stay away from core subsystems (such as memory management) since those require a lot of expertise, and go with what you are most interested in. In my case I chose the DRM subsystem in charge of managing everything related to rendering graphics, a topic I find very interesting, and IIO Subsystem because I wanted to learn how to write device drivers2 by starting with the simplest ones. I also checked the Rust for Linux project, because, as you can see in a lot of other posts on this blog I am really interested in the Rust programming language!

The General Experience

The program is designed to be self-driven on purpose, because it is what open source contributors experience. This means that you are in charge of finding where to contribute, learn what is needed to generate a patch and send it to the mailing list.

Since it is a self-driven program, a lot doubts about different topics will surely arise. To solve them, a one-hour weekly meeting is held where mentors will answer questions and explain different things. Along with those, some other things that really helped me were to ask questions directly to other more experienced mentees (some people in the program already have some kernel development experience) in a common discord channel, read the mailing list periodically and read the documentation of the subsystems I chose.

The program also prohibits the use of AI, and this is a good thing. Using AI interrupts the learning process. To learn, you need to struggle.

The Myth & The Reality

There is a myth that the Linux kernel community is a harsh one. That when you send a patch you will get no friendly suggestions or you will be insulted. That is not true, at all. Maintainers are people too, and they are usually busy, their feedback is concrete and goes straight to the point for the sake of efficiency, but no one will mistreat you. Also, getting feedback from experienced kernel developers is of immense value.

The community expects that you invest time to understand what you are doing, put effort on the patches you send, test them thoroughly and be willing to continue working on them when you receive feedback. Be respectful of other people’s time.

From Small To Not-So-Small Patches

My first patch was a very small one: an optimization in the Rust’s OPP module that removes intermediate symbols generated by clang for methods that are just a wrapper of C functions. I still remember the sensation when I received the e-mail confirming that it was applied! More small patches followed this one, but as I became more familiar with the code (and the subsystems I chose) I increased the complexity of the things I worked on. It is recommended to start sending patches early on the program. Don’t be afraid to send simple ones, you have to start somewhere.

To make my life easier, I created a scrum-like (ugh) board to follow my progress:

As you can see, there are a lot of Rejected patches. Most of them were rejected because they were not ready yet to be merged into the kernel. Each of those rejections teached me something that I did not know or did not take into account before sending them.

You can check my list of accepted patches in the kernel here. At the moment of writing this post, this is what git log --author=nico.antinori.7@gmail.com --pretty --format=oneline gives me:

i2c: rust: mark I2cAdapter methods as inline
rust: pin-init: mark `pin_init::zeroed` and `Zeroable::zeroed` as `#[inline]`
rust: pin-init: docs: link `Zeroable::zeroed` and `pin_init::zeroed` in documentation
rust_binder: use pin_init::zeroed for file_operations initialization
usb: rust: mark Device and Interface methods as inline
drm/amdgpu: Inline drm_simple_encoder_init()
drm/panel: novatek-nt37801: Use mipi_dsi_*_multi() functions
rust: iommu: replace core::mem::zeroed with Zeroable::zeroed
usb: rust: Use pin_init::zeroed for usb_device_id initialization
gpu: nova-core: vbios: parse structs via zerocopy
(tag: rust-i2c-7.1-rc7, i2c/rust-i2c-fixes) rust: i2c: fix I2cAdapter refcounts double increment
(tag: opp-updates-7.2) opp: rust: mark OPP methods as inline

And in linux-next tree there are three more:

rust_binder: simplify Result<()> uses
iio: humidity: am2315: add support for am2320
dt-bindings: trivial-devices: add Aosong AM2315 and AM2320 chips

Note: Commit hashes were removed for the sake of redability.

Currently, I am working in a DRM driver for the CH1115 controller, a simple driver, but that requires dealing with different subsystems (i2c, DRM) and different kernel APIs.

Conclusion

I had a really good experience going through this program. The chance of being part of the kernel community and being able to contribute to such an important project is priceless to me.

I am very grateful to my mentors Shuah Khan, Brigham Campbell and Jori Koolstra for all the patience and guidance. The program definitely made things easier, seeing people struggling with the same things as I, and having mentors to help with those struggles and the general process of becoming a kernel developer is highly encouraging. Thanks to them and the program I achieved my long time goal of contributing to the Linux kernel.

If you are planning to participate, do not hesitate. You’ll sharpen your programming skills, learn how to be part of the linux kernel community, and receive expert feedback on your work!

My plan is, of course, to continue contributing.

  1. You can also check the Kernel Newbies program. ↩︎

  2. The Setting up a Linux Kernel dev environment with Raspberry Pi, U-Boot, TFTP and NFS post is the process I followed to set up my Raspberry Pi 3b+ as a work station for developing drivers and testing things. ↩︎

item.title: Setting up a Linux Kernel dev environment with Raspberry Pi, U-Boot, TFTP and NFS
item.description:
I am writing this guide basically to use it from time to time if I need it. For this to work you need:

  • Raspberry Pi (in this guide we use 3b+, but I believe anyone should do the trick).
  • Micro SD card.
  • SD card reader in the host machine.
  • USB keyboard (can be a wireless one with a dongle, but it should not be Bluetooth).

The host machine of this guide runs Debian 13. It is assumed that you know how to compile a custom kernel. I won’t enter in much detail about the commands used here, because, as I said earlier, I am basically writing this guide for my future self.
item.content:encoded:
I am writing this guide basically to use it from time to time if I need it. For this to work you need:

  • Raspberry Pi (in this guide we use 3b+, but I believe anyone should do the trick).
  • Micro SD card.
  • SD card reader in the host machine.
  • USB keyboard (can be a wireless one with a dongle, but it should not be Bluetooth).

The host machine of this guide runs Debian 13. It is assumed that you know how to compile a custom kernel. I won’t enter in much detail about the commands used here, because, as I said earlier, I am basically writing this guide for my future self.

Install Raspberry Pi Os

The first thing you need to do is to install Raspberry OS in the SD card. For this I recommend using the Raspberry Pi Imager, since it is the easiest way to install the OS and you can choose whatever option suits you better (in my case I use the minimal install).

Copying rootfs to host

Once you have the system installed in your SD card, you’ll need to copy the rootfs partition to a folder in your host system. This folder will be the rootfs partition when booting through NFS.

First check the card’s partitions:

$ lsblk
sdc           8:32   1  14.8G  0 disk
├─sdc1        8:33   1   512M  0 part
└─sdc2        8:34   1  14.3G  0 part

In my case, the rootfs is sdc2, I proceed to mount it:

$ mkdir /tmp/rpi_rootfs
$ sudo mount /dev/sdc2 /tmp/rpi_rootfs

And then, synchronize it to a folder in the host system

$ sudo rsync -axHAWX --numeric-ids /tmp/rpi_rootfs <HOST_ROOTFS>

where <HOST_ROOTFS> is the directory where you will place the rootfs in your host machine.

Compile and install U-Boot

U-Boot will allow us to boot a kernel image served via TFTP and mount a root file system served via NFS. First, you need to clone the repository:

$ git clone https://github.com/u-boot/u-boot.git

Before compiling it, you need to create a configuration specifically for the board you are going to use for development. In my case it is a Raspberry Pi 3b+, so I needed to execute the following command to generate the configuration:

$ cd u-boot
$ make rpi_3_b_plus_defconfig

Note: Check the configs folder to see the available board configs.

Once the configuration is in place, compile the binary:

$ make ARCH=arm CROSS_COMPILE="aarch64-linux-gnu-" -j$(nproc)

This will leave the U-Boot binaries in the repository’s root directory. The needed file is called u-boot.bin. You’ll have to copy it to the boot partition of the SD card:

$ mkdir /tmp/rpi_bootfs
$ sudo mount /dev/sdc1 /tmp/rpi_bootfs
$ cp u-boot.bin /tmp/rpi_bootfs

Later, modify the config.txt, also located in the boot partition. Add the following at the end of the named file:

[all]
enable_uart=1
kernel=u-boot.bin

With this modification, instead of booting the system, the Raspberry will boot into U-Boot.

After this step, the SD card is not needed anymore. Unmount the partitions with:

$ sudo umount /dev/sdc1
$ sudo umount /dev/sdc2

And put it in the Raspberry Pi.

Configuring TFTP

TFTP is used to load kernel images over Ethernet. This is very useful when working with the latest kernels, since it allows you to compile new versions and boot them really quickly. First, you need to install dnsmasq package:

$ sudo apt-get install dnsmasq

Then, create the directory where the kernel image will be served:

$ sudo mkdir -p /var/tftpd

Configure dnsmasq by adding the following to /etc/dnsmasq.conf:

listen-address=<HOST_MACHINE_IP_ADDRESS>
dhcp-range=192.168.1.50,192.168.1.200,24h
enable-tftp
tftp-root=/var/tftpd

Note: 192.168.1.0/24 is the subnet where my host machine lives.

And restart the service:

$ sudo service dnsmasq restart

Configuring NFS

Now it is time to serve the rootfs folder. First, as with the other tools, you need to install it:

$ sudo apt install nfs-kernel-server

Then add the following to the /etc/exports config file:

<HOST_ROOTFS> 192.168.1.0/24(rw,no_root_squash,async,no_subtree_check)

Export the new NFS file system and restart the service:

sudo exportfs -rav
sudo systemctl restart nfs-kernel-server

Booting the system

I assume you have a new kernel image you want to boot, so we need to prepare the kernel image and its modules before doing anything.

All the steps in the following subsections are executed from the kernel source root directory.

Before booting

Before doing anything, you must disable mounting the rootfs from the SD card. This must be done once, but it is an important step. Open the file located at <HOST_ROOTFS>/etc/fstab and comment the following line:

...
# PARTUUID=f619f15c-02  /               ext4    defaults,noatime  0       1
...

Note: The UUID will be different in your case.

Build a new kernel

  1. Build the kernel image, modules and device tree bindings:

    $ make ARCH=arm64 CROSS_COMPILE="aarch64-linux-gnu-" -j$(nproc) Image modules dtbs

  2. Place the new kernel image in the TFTP directory:

    $ sudo cp arch/arm64/boot/Image /var/tftpd

  3. Install the new kernel modules in the host root fs folder:

    $ sudo make ARCH=arm64 CROSS_COMPILE="aarch64-linux-gnu-" INSTALL_MOD_PATH=<HOST_ROOTFS> modules_install

Note: Device tree bindings were compiled but not copied anywhere because they must be placed in the boot partition. If you need to modify the device tree bindings, you can copy the compiled dtbo file to the home folder and move it from there using ssh.

Booting up the Raspberry Pi

It is time! Now that we have everything in place in the host machine, plug your Raspberry Pi to a USB keyboard, a display screen and start it. If everything goes right, you will boot into the U-Boot prompt console after some failed boot trials. This is ok, now it is time to configure U-Boot to use the kernel image in the TFTP directory and mount as the root file system the one that we are serving through NFS.

Testing the setup

Before making the U-Boot configuration “permanent” (you can change it later :P), I believe it is a good idea to test it. Execute the following commands inside the U-Boot prompt:

U-Boot> dhcp
U-Boot> setenv serverip <HOST_MACHINE_IP_ADDRESS>
U-Boot> tftp ${kernel_addr_r} Image
U-Boot> fdt addr ${fdt_addr}
U-Boot> fdt set /chosen bootargs "console=serial0,115200 console=tty1 root=/dev/nfs nfsroot=<HOST_MACHINE_IP_ADDRESS>:<HOST_ROOTFS>,nfsvers=4.1, rw ip=dhcp"
U-Boot> booti ${kernel_addr_r} - ${fdt_addr}

If everything is configured correctly, you should boot into a new Raspberry Pi Os installation. Log-in with the user and password you specified in the Raspberry Pi Imager.

To check if you are really using the NFS root file system, in your host machine, create a file in your Raspberry’s user home directory:

$ touch <HOST_ROOTFS>/home/<YOUR_USERNAME>/TEST_NFS

and check if you can see it in the Raspberry Pi TTY using ls.

Automatically booting using TFTP and NFS

To avoid entering the commands every time you boot, you can save the environment. To make this configuration “permanent”, enter the following commands into the U-Boot console:

U-Boot> setenv autoload no
U-Boot> setenv netboot 'dhcp; setenv serverip <HOST_MACHINE_IP_ADDRESS>; tftp ${kernel_addr_r} Image; fdt addr ${fdt_addr}; fdt set /chosen bootargs "console=serial0,115200 console=tty1 root=/dev/nfs nfsroot=<HOST_MACHINE_IP_ADDRESS>:<HOST_ROOTFS>,nfsvers=4.1, rw ip=dhcp"; bootconfig; booti ${kernel_addr_r} - ${fdt_addr}'
U-Boot> setenv bootcmd "run netboot"
U-Boot> saveenv

Conclusion

You can develop using the SD card alone, but this setup is way more convenient because it makes working with different kernel versions, different devices and kernel modules easier. I hope you find this guide useful.

  • Buildroot and U-boot on Raspberry Pi
  • Booting RAM disk images over Ethernet
